stem: Why do many autistic self-advocates and members of Deaf culture prefer identity-first language (such as 'autistic person') over person-first language?

options.text: Because they regard it as the terminology required in international human rights treaties.
options.rationale: The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities uses person-first language such as 'persons with disabilities', and no human rights treaty requires identity-first wording.

options.text: Because they regard it as a clearer way to name the specific diagnosis.
options.rationale: Both forms name the same diagnosis; the preference is about identity, not about clarity of diagnosis.

options.text: Because they regard disability as an inherent and valued part of who they are rather than a separate trait.
options.rationale: Identity-first language presents disability as an integral and valued part of a person's identity rather than a detached trait.

options.text: Because they regard person-first phrasing as suited to physical rather than cognitive disabilities.
options.rationale: Person-first phrasing is used across disability types, including cognitive and mental health conditions, so it is not restricted to physical disabilities.

explanation: Person-first language is widely recommended to avoid defining a person by a disability, and it is the form used in the UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities. Some self-advocates, including many autistic people and members of Deaf culture, prefer identity-first language because they experience disability as a positive and inseparable part of who they are. In direct communication, it is best to ask the person which form they prefer.
